query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In chromium-bearing steels, refining the microstructure to increase grain boundary density accelerates chromium diffusion to the surface, thereby forming a uniform, Cr-enriched passive oxide film that resists localized corrosion in chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional, coarse-grained stainless or duplex steels containing a sufficient amount of chromium (e.g., DS2205) with typical passivation behavior.
generation.intervention: Apply processing (such as severe plastic deformation or high-pressure torsion) to produce an ultrafine-grained (UFG) microstructure without altering the steel’s composition.
generation.conditions: Test specimens in corrosive environments representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications (e.g., high-temperature aqueous chloride solutions or molten salt environments) under controlled electrochemical potentials.
generation.structural_mediator: An increased density of grain boundaries in the UFG microstructure that serves as fast diffusion pathways for chromium.
generation.mechanism: The high concentration of grain boundaries in UFG steels promotes rapid diffusion and segregation of chromium atoms to the surface, leading to the formation of a thicker and more uniform Cr-rich passive oxide film that protects against pitting and general corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarse-grained steels, the UFG steels will exhibit lower corrosion current densities, enhanced Cr enrichment within the passive film (as verified by XPS or SKP analysis), and reduced pitting and surface degradation under identical corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained steels of identical chemical composition that form a less uniform or less Cr-enriched passive film and display higher corrosion rates under the same test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for chromium-containing stainless and duplex steels in environments typical of chemical processing and nuclear-power applications, but may not apply to steels with very low Cr content or those that form nonprotective films.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in corrosion rate reduction and film uniformity between UFG and coarse-grained steels will vary with the precise corrosive medium, temperature, and exposure time. The optimal grain size and corresponding Cr diffusion rate are also not precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel specimens with identical chromium content and chemical composition: one set processed to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure via severe plastic deformation and the other retained in a coarse-grained state. Subject both sets to identical, controlled corrosive environments (e.g., high-temperature chloride solutions or simulated molten salt conditions) and monitor their electrochemical behavior.
measurements: Corrosion current density using potentiodynamic polarization tests
Surface and passive film composition analysis via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or scanning Kelvin probe (SKP)
Microstructural characterization for grain size and grain boundary density via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) or transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Surface morphology assessment using scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained specimens do not show statistically significant improvements—such as reduced corrosion current densities, higher Cr content in the passive film, or lower incidence of pitting—compared to their coarse-grained counterparts under identical test conditions, the hypothesis that increased grain boundary–mediated Cr diffusion improves corrosion resistance is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed.
